title: 108 PRs in eight days: Accidentally discovering loop engineering | Brittany Ellich | Offprint
excerpt: How I shipped 108 PRs in eight days with an agent working my task board: the loop engineering setup, constraints, and lessons that made it work.
content_html:
For the last week or so I've had an agent working my task board. It picks up a task, writes the code in an isolated worktree, opens a PR, gets CI green, responds to review feedback, and parks the result somewhere I can test it. Then it sleeps for a while and does it again. As of this morning, 108 tasks have gone through it in about eight days. Compared to my previous average of 5-10 PRs per week, that's a pretty substantial change.

There are a few things that enable this to work well. I am on a team that is small and is cooking right now. I'm not the only person on my team moving fast, and we have a very high level of trust. We don't have a mandatory rule that another person looks at the code, too, which helps tremendously. I still get input from a coworker if I'm unsure about something, but not having to wait on someone else's timing to merge and get stuff done is huge.

I posted about this on Bluesky recently ("unless you're shipping nuclear safety code, you probably don't need a human reviewer for your PRs") and the most consistent pushback wasn't about AI review quality at all. It was that PR review is how teams stay aligned and how junior engineers learn. I think that's fair, and it's exactly why the team context matters here: on a two-to-three person team that talks every day, alignment happens in conversation, not in a review tab. If you're on a bigger team, or mentoring juniors, that might not work as well. I also want to be clear that I didn't remove the human from review. I moved where the review happens. I still look at every change, but at the testing-and-outcome level instead of line by line in a PR.

We also don't have continuous deployment (CD) set up. That's a weird thing for me to say as a positive, because for a very long time that was a hallmark of good software engineering practices... but with me shipping 108 PRs in a week, I actually have been thinking differently. Now I prefer CI plus a preview/stage environment, releasing a batch of work at once instead of shipping a new build to users on every merge. It still averages 2 or so changes in production per day, but it dramatically limits the surface area for when things can go wrong. It means I only have to regression test once or twice per day, and can handle bugs early on, before they're in front of users.

It turns out that what I've been iterating on for my personal process has a name: loop engineering. Addy Osmani coined the term in June, building on things Boris Cherny (Claude Code) and Peter Steinberger had been saying about designing the system that prompts your agents instead of typing every prompt yourself. Most of what I've read about it stops at "give it a clear goal and a turn cap." That advice is fine, but I found for my own use case I need more than just that.

My three layers to loop engineering

The system has a protocol, a loop, and a worker.

The protocol is a markdown file with the rules: what each status means, what happens in what order on each pass, what gets merged and what doesn't. It lives next to the board rather than in the repo, so editing the rules and editing the board are the same act. I keep my board separate from the main repos I work in, so that I can work in multiple repos from a single source.

The loop reads the board, runs gh, updates task frontmatter, and dispatches work. It writes no code. It doesn't touch the repository working tree at all.

The worker writes code in its own isolated worktree and reports back with a small structured block. It never touches the board, and it never talks to me directly.

The board is a folder filled with markdown task files

My first version was a single markdown file with a table in it. That lasted about a day, as I realized it caused a lot of collisions between me adding to the board and the board updating itself.

One markdown note per task fixes this structurally, and works really nicely with Obsidian's Bases, which provides the actual board structure, with a bit of frontmatter to keep things tidy. We only collide when we both touch the same task, which is rare and obvious when it happens. As a bonus, a stray | in my own notes can't break the whole system anymore, and the board becomes queryable as data instead of something that has to be parsed as text.

The same reasoning applies one layer down: the loop is the only writer to the board and to the memory file. Workers hand results back and the loop records them. Three agents running concurrently can't corrupt a file that only one process is allowed to write to.

The main checkout is mine

Every task runs in a subagent with worktree isolation, branched from the repo's default branch, not from whatever I happen to have checked out. My half-finished local state never leaks into a task, and a task's edits never show up in my tree while I'm in the middle of testing something.

I test tasks that are ready to test in my locally checked out branch. From there I can review the code, make changes myself, or add changes to the task for the agent to take and change on the next loop.

The loop has to be able to stop

I run my loops with Claude Code's /loop functionality with no interval.

Giving /loop an interval turns it into a cron job: it runs until you kill it or it expires, and it can't end itself. Bare /loop without an interval is self-paced. It picks its own delay after each pass, short while a PR is active and long once things go quiet, and it can end the loop entirely once the board says nothing can move without me. This lets me set up a bunch of issues for it to churn through and run through them over night, creating a nice backlog of things for me to test with test instructions included for the next day.

The protocol has an explicit stop condition, written as a list of things that must all be true: nothing in progress, nothing waiting on CI, nothing merge-ready, and every remaining task either waiting on me or finished. When that holds, the loop says what it's waiting on in one line and stops until I start it again, meaning that I finish using tokens as soon as it runs out of work.

Memory, with a hard cap

The loop keeps a memory file of what the process has learned: facts about the codebase that cost a worker real time, preferences I've stated more than once, defects that keep coming back. Each entry carries a confirmation count and a date, and every dispatch pastes the memory into the worker's prompt. It forces the unwritten stuff to get written down, with a count attached, so we know how often a problem is run into and resolve it, instead of continuing to get stuck.

Once the confirmation count on a bug or issue reaches a certain point, fixing it becomes its own task. For example, workers kept getting stuck on a stale skill that was saved in the repo, until they eventually made a task to remove the skill. That makes the entire process more efficient over time, and frees up a memory slot for something else.

Using a hard cap keeps the memory list streamlined and requires that the system make tradeoffs to find the most relevant pieces to keep. Memories get loaded into each worker as they work, and I want to manage that context to keep it small.

It’s me, hi, I'm the bottleneck, it’s me

My board right now has zero tasks queued and eight waiting for me to test them, which means it's waiting on me to do the testing and to add more work to the queue. Where I'm spending my time gives me good insight on how to make the loop even better.

Several people in that Bluesky thread predicted this shift: that human effort would move from reviewing code to reviewing specs and issue definitions. That matches exactly where my time went. Both ends of my pipeline are spec work now: deciding what goes in the queue, and verifying what comes out. It almost feels like being a software engineer in 2026 is just being a product manager and QA.

For example, I ended up adding a skill to create a task so that I can explore an issue with Claude, like perhaps some errors in our error log or something operating slowly, so that Claude can quickly add tasks to the backlog as we explore. Trying to reduce the bottleneck of adding the right items to the queue is the next area I’m iterating on.

Automating the testing and verification stage is the other area I'm looking into. How can I create an automation that will do the manual review process before even handing it over, to check things like accessibility, how things look on a mobile device, or whether there are any regressions? That way my QA stage continues to get shorter.

How to get started

I'm open sourcing my loop setup for you to try out if you want. Everyone's process is different, so you may even want to start from scratch.

As a first step, I recommend writing down what "done" looks like before you write anything else. Every good decision in my protocol came from being forced to define a state precisely: the task completed, green CI, and an approved AI code review. From there you can start slowly working out from "done". On the frontend, how you go from a task or issue to a completed PR, and on the backend how you make sure everything gets prepared for you to review.

If you give this a try I’d love to see how it works for you! Reach out and let me know.

blocks.html_en: My first version was a single markdown file with a table in it. That lasted about a day, as I realized it caused a lot of collisions between me adding to the board and the board updating itself.

sentences.en: My first version was a single markdown file with a table in it.
sentences.zh: 我的第一个版本是一个带有表格的单个 Markdown 文件。

sentences.en: That lasted about a day, as I realized it caused a lot of collisions between me adding to the board and the board updating itself.
sentences.zh: 这持续了大约一天，因为我意识到这在我向董事会添加内容和董事会更新自身之间引起了很多冲突。

blocks.html_en: One markdown note per task fixes this structurally, and works really nicely with Obsidian's Bases, which provides the actual board structure, with a bit of frontmatter to keep things tidy. We only collide when we both touch the same task, which is rare and obvious when it happens. As a bonus, a stray | in my own notes can't break the whole system anymore, and the board becomes queryable as data instead of something that has to be parsed as text.

sentences.en: One markdown note per task fixes this structurally, and works really nicely with Obsidian's Bases, which provides the actual board structure, with a bit of frontmatter to keep things tidy.
sentences.zh: 每个任务的一个降价注释在结构上修复了这个问题，并且与 Obsidian 的 Bases 配合得非常好，它提供了实际的板结构，并带有一些前言以保持整洁。

sentences.en: We only collide when we both touch the same task, which is rare and obvious when it happens.
sentences.zh: 只有当我们都接触同一个任务时，我们才会发生冲突，这种情况很少见，但发生时却很明显。

sentences.en: As a bonus, a stray | in my own notes can't break the whole system anymore, and the board becomes queryable as data instead of something that has to be parsed as text.
sentences.zh: 作为奖励，流浪者 |在我自己的笔记中，不能再破坏整个系统，并且董事会可以作为数据进行查询，而不是必须解析为文本的内容。

blocks.html_en: The same reasoning applies one layer down: the loop is the only writer to the board and to the memory file. Workers hand results back and the loop records them. Three agents running concurrently can't corrupt a file that only one process is allowed to write to.

sentences.en: The same reasoning applies one layer down: the loop is the only writer to the board and to the memory file.
sentences.zh: 同样的推理也适用于下一层：循环是电路板和内存文件的唯一写入器。

sentences.en: Workers hand results back and the loop records them.
sentences.zh: 工作人员将结果返回并由循环记录它们。

sentences.en: Three agents running concurrently can't corrupt a file that only one process is allowed to write to.
sentences.zh: 同时运行的三个代理不会损坏只允许一个进程写入的文件。

blocks.html_en: The main checkout is mine

sentences.en: The main checkout is mine
sentences.zh: 主要结账是我的

blocks.html_en: Every task runs in a subagent with worktree isolation, branched from the repo's default branch, not from whatever I happen to have checked out. My half-finished local state never leaks into a task, and a task's edits never show up in my tree while I'm in the middle of testing something.

sentences.en: Every task runs in a subagent with worktree isolation, branched from the repo's default branch, not from whatever I happen to have checked out.
sentences.zh: 每个任务都在具有工作树隔离的子代理中运行，从存储库的默认分支分支，而不是从我碰巧签出的任何分支分支。

sentences.en: My half-finished local state never leaks into a task, and a task's edits never show up in my tree while I'm in the middle of testing something.
sentences.zh: 我的半完成本地状态永远不会泄漏到任务中，并且当我正在测试某些内容时，任务的编辑永远不会显示在我的树中。

blocks.html_en: I test tasks that are ready to test in my locally checked out branch. From there I can review the code, make changes myself, or add changes to the task for the agent to take and change on the next loop.

sentences.en: I test tasks that are ready to test in my locally checked out branch.
sentences.zh: 我测试准备在本地签出的分支中测试的任务。

sentences.en: From there I can review the code, make changes myself, or add changes to the task for the agent to take and change on the next loop.
sentences.zh: 从那里，我可以检查代码，自己进行更改，或者向任务添加更改，以便代理在下一个循环中执行和更改。

blocks.html_en: The loop has to be able to stop

sentences.en: The loop has to be able to stop
sentences.zh: 循环必须能够停止

blocks.html_en: I run my loops with Claude Code's /loop functionality with no interval.

sentences.en: I run my loops with Claude Code's /loop functionality with no interval.
sentences.zh: 我使用 Claude Code 的 /loop 功能无间隔地运行循环。

blocks.html_en: Giving /loop an interval turns it into a cron job: it runs until you kill it or it expires, and it can't end itself. Bare /loop without an interval is self-paced. It picks its own delay after each pass, short while a PR is active and long once things go quiet, and it can end the loop entirely once the board says nothing can move without me. This lets me set up a bunch of issues for it to churn through and run through them over night, creating a nice backlog of things for me to test with test instructions included for the next day.

sentences.en: Giving /loop an interval turns it into a cron job: it runs until you kill it or it expires, and it can't end itself.
sentences.zh: 给 /loop 一个间隔将其变成一个 cron 作业：它会一直运行，直到您杀死它或它过期，并且它无法自行结束。

sentences.en: Bare /loop without an interval is self-paced.
sentences.zh: 没有间隔的裸/循环是自定进度的。

sentences.en: It picks its own delay after each pass, short while a PR is active and long once things go quiet, and it can end the loop entirely once the board says nothing can move without me.
sentences.zh: 每次通过后，它都会选择自己的延迟，在 PR 处于活动状态时会短暂延迟，而一旦事情变得安静，它就会选择很长的延迟，并且一旦董事会说没有我就没有任何东西可以移动，它可以完全结束循环。

sentences.en: This lets me set up a bunch of issues for it to churn through and run through them over night, creating a nice backlog of things for me to test with test instructions included for the next day.
sentences.zh: 这让我可以设置一堆问题，让它在晚上进行处理并运行它们，为我创建一个很好的积压事项，以便我使用第二天的测试说明进行测试。

blocks.html_en: The protocol has an explicit stop condition, written as a list of things that must all be true: nothing in progress, nothing waiting on CI, nothing merge-ready, and every remaining task either waiting on me or finished. When that holds, the loop says what it's waiting on in one line and stops until I start it again, meaning that I finish using tokens as soon as it runs out of work.

sentences.zh: 该协议有一个明确的停止条件，写成一系列必须全部为真的事情：没有任何进展，没有任何等待 CI，没有任何合并就绪，并且每个剩余的任务要么在等待我，要么已完成。

sentences.en: When that holds, the loop says what it's waiting on in one line and stops until I start it again, meaning that I finish using tokens as soon as it runs out of work.
sentences.zh: 当这种情况成立时，循环会在一行中说出它正在等待的内容，然后停止，直到我再次启动它，这意味着一旦它用完工作，我就会完成使用令牌。

blocks.html_en: Memory, with a hard cap

sentences.en: Memory, with a hard cap
sentences.zh: 内存，带硬上限

blocks.html_en: The loop keeps a memory file of what the process has learned: facts about the codebase that cost a worker real time, preferences I've stated more than once, defects that keep coming back. Each entry carries a confirmation count and a date, and every dispatch pastes the memory into the worker's prompt. It forces the unwritten stuff to get written down, with a count attached, so we know how often a problem is run into and resolve it, instead of continuing to get stuck.

sentences.en: The loop keeps a memory file of what the process has learned: facts about the codebase that cost a worker real time, preferences I've stated more than once, defects that keep coming back.
sentences.zh: 该循环保存了进程所学到的内容的内存文件：有关使工作人员实时花费时间的代码库的事实、我不止一次说过的偏好、不断出现的缺陷。

sentences.en: Each entry carries a confirmation count and a date, and every dispatch pastes the memory into the worker's prompt.
sentences.zh: 每个条目都带有确认计数和日期，每次调度都会将内存粘贴到工作人员的提示中。

sentences.en: It forces the unwritten stuff to get written down, with a count attached, so we know how often a problem is run into and resolve it, instead of continuing to get stuck.
sentences.zh: 它迫使未写下的东西被写下来，并附上计数，这样我们就知道遇到问题的频率并解决它，而不是继续陷入困境。

blocks.html_en: Once the confirmation count on a bug or issue reaches a certain point, fixing it becomes its own task. For example, workers kept getting stuck on a stale skill that was saved in the repo, until they eventually made a task to remove the skill. That makes the entire process more efficient over time, and frees up a memory slot for something else.

sentences.en: Once the confirmation count on a bug or issue reaches a certain point, fixing it becomes its own task.

sentences.en: That makes the entire process more efficient over time, and frees up a memory slot for something else.
sentences.zh: 随着时间的推移，这使得整个过程更加高效，并为其他事情释放内存插槽。

blocks.html_en: Using a hard cap keeps the memory list streamlined and requires that the system make tradeoffs to find the most relevant pieces to keep. Memories get loaded into each worker as they work, and I want to manage that context to keep it small.

sentences.zh: 使用硬上限可以简化内存列表，并要求系统进行权衡以找到要保留的最相关的部分。

sentences.en: Memories get loaded into each worker as they work, and I want to manage that context to keep it small.
sentences.zh: 每个工作人员在工作时都会加载记忆，我想管理该上下文以使其保持较小的规模。

blocks.html_en: It’s me, hi, I'm the bottleneck, it’s me

That matches exactly where my time went. Both ends of my pipeline are spec work now: deciding what goes in the queue, and verifying what comes out. It almost feels like being a software engineer in 2026 is just being a product manager and QA.

content_html_zh:
在过去一周左右的时间里，我有一名代理人在我的任务板上工作。 它会选择一个任务，在一个独立的工作树中编写代码，打开 PR，使 CI 绿色，响应审查反馈，并将结果存放在我可以测试的地方。 然后它会休眠一段时间并再次执行此操作。 截至今天上午，大约八天内完成了108项任务。 与我之前平均每周 5-10 个 PR 相比，这是一个相当大的变化。

有一些因素可以使其发挥良好作用。 我所在的团队规模很小，现在正在做饭。 我不是团队中唯一行动迅速的人，而且我们之间有着非常高的信任度。 我们没有强制要求其他人也查看代码，这有很大帮助。 如果我对某件事不确定，我仍然会从同事那里得到意见，但不必等待其他人的时间来合并并完成工作，这是巨大的。

我最近在 Bluesky 上发布了相关内容（“除非您要发布核安全代码，否则您的 PR 可能不需要人工审核员”），而最一致的反对根本不是关于人工智能审核质量。 PR 审查是团队保持一致以及初级工程师学习的方式。 我认为这是公平的，这正是团队环境在这里重要的原因：在每天交谈的两到三人团队中，一致性发生在对话中，而不是在审核选项卡中。 如果你在一个更大的团队中，或者指导后辈，这可能不太有效。 我还想澄清的是，我并没有将人类从审核中删除。 我搬到了审查发生的地方。 我仍然关注每一个变化，但是是在测试和结果层面，而不是在 PR 中逐行关注。

我们也没有设置持续部署 (CD)。 对我来说，说这是积极的事情是一件奇怪的事情，因为很长一段时间以来，这是良好软件工程实践的标志...... 但当我在一周内发布 108 个 PR 时，我实际上一直在思考不同的问题。 现在我更喜欢 CI 加上预览/阶段环境，一次性发布一批工作，而不是在每次合并时向用户发送新版本。 虽然每天的产量平均仍会发生 2 次左右的变化，但它极大地限制了出现问题时的处理范围。 这意味着我每天只需进行一到两次回归测试，并且可以在错误出现在用户面前之前尽早处理它们。

事实证明，我一直在为我的个人流程迭代的东西有一个名字：循环工程。 Addy Osmani 在 6 月创造了这个术语，其基础是 Boris Cherny（Claude Code）和 Peter Steinberger 一直在谈论的关于设计提示您的代理的系统而不是自己输入每个提示的内容。 我读到的关于它的大部分内容都停留在“给它一个明确的目标和一个转变上限”。 这个建议很好，但我发现对于我自己的用例，我需要的不仅仅是这些。

我的三层循环工程

该系统有一个协议、一个循环和一个工作线程。

该协议是一个包含规则的 Markdown 文件：每个状态的含义是什么，每次传递以什么顺序发生什么，什么被合并，什么不被合并。 它位于看板旁边而不是存储库中，因此编辑规则和编辑看板是同一行为。 我将我的董事会与我工作的主要存储库分开，以便我可以在来自单一来源的多个存储库中工作。

该循环读取棋盘，运行 gh，更新任务 frontmatter，并分派工作。 它不写任何代码。 它根本不触及存储库工作树。

工作人员在自己独立的工作树中编写代码，并用一个小的结构化块进行报告。 它从不接触棋盘，也从不直接与我对话。

board是一个充满markdown任务文件的文件夹

我的第一个版本是一个带有表格的单个 Markdown 文件。 这持续了大约一天，因为我意识到这在我向董事会添加内容和董事会更新自身之间引起了很多冲突。

每个任务的一个降价注释在结构上修复了这个问题，并且与 Obsidian 的 Bases 配合得非常好，它提供了实际的板结构，并带有一些前言以保持整洁。 只有当我们都接触同一个任务时，我们才会发生冲突，这种情况很少见，但发生时却很明显。 作为奖励，流浪者 |在我自己的笔记中，不能再破坏整个系统，并且董事会可以作为数据进行查询，而不是必须解析为文本的内容。

同样的推理也适用于下一层：循环是电路板和内存文件的唯一写入器。 工作人员将结果返回并由循环记录它们。 同时运行的三个代理不会损坏只允许一个进程写入的文件。

主要结账是我的

每个任务都在具有工作树隔离的子代理中运行，从存储库的默认分支分支，而不是从我碰巧签出的任何分支分支。 我的半完成本地状态永远不会泄漏到任务中，并且当我正在测试某些内容时，任务的编辑永远不会显示在我的树中。

我测试准备在本地签出的分支中测试的任务。 从那里，我可以检查代码，自己进行更改，或者向任务添加更改，以便代理在下一个循环中执行和更改。

循环必须能够停止

我使用 Claude Code 的 /loop 功能无间隔地运行循环。

给 /loop 一个间隔将其变成一个 cron 作业：它会一直运行，直到您杀死它或它过期，并且它无法自行结束。 没有间隔的裸/循环是自定进度的。 每次通过后，它都会选择自己的延迟，在 PR 处于活动状态时会短暂延迟，而一旦事情变得安静，它就会选择很长的延迟，并且一旦董事会说没有我就没有任何东西可以移动，它可以完全结束循环。 这让我可以设置一堆问题，让它在晚上进行处理并运行它们，为我创建一个很好的积压事项，以便我使用第二天的测试说明进行测试。

该协议有一个明确的停止条件，写成一系列必须全部为真的事情：没有任何进展，没有任何等待 CI，没有任何合并就绪，并且每个剩余的任务要么在等待我，要么已完成。 当这种情况成立时，循环会在一行中说出它正在等待的内容，然后停止，直到我再次启动它，这意味着一旦它用完工作，我就会完成使用令牌。

内存，带硬上限

该循环保存了进程所学到的内容的内存文件：有关使工作人员实时花费时间的代码库的事实、我不止一次说过的偏好、不断出现的缺陷。 每个条目都带有确认计数和日期，每次调度都会将内存粘贴到工作人员的提示中。 它迫使未写下的东西被写下来，并附上计数，这样我们就知道遇到问题的频率并解决它，而不是继续陷入困境。

一旦错误或问题的确认计数达到一定程度，修复它就成为自己的任务。 例如，工作人员不断陷入存储库中保存的过时技能上，直到他们最终执行删除该技能的任务。 随着时间的推移，这使得整个过程更加高效，并为其他事情释放内存插槽。

使用硬上限可以简化内存列表，并要求系统进行权衡以找到要保留的最相关的部分。 每个工作人员在工作时都会加载记忆，我想管理该上下文以使其保持较小的规模。

是我，嗨，我是瓶颈，是我

我的主板现在有零个任务在排队，八个任务等待我测试它们，这意味着它正在等待我进行测试并向队列添加更多工作。 我花时间的地方让我对如何使循环变得更好有了很好的了解。

Bluesky 线程中的几个人预测了这种转变：人类的工作将从审查代码转向审查规范和问题定义。 这完全符合我的时间去向。 我的管道的两端现在都是规范工作：决定队列中的内容，并验证输出的内容。 感觉 2026 年的软件工程师就只是产品经理和 QA。

例如，我最终添加了一项创建任务的技能，以便我可以与 Claude 一起探索问题，例如错误日志中的一些错误或运行缓慢的内容，以便 Claude 可以在我们探索时快速将任务添加到待办事项中。 尝试减少向队列添加正确项目的瓶颈是我要迭代的下一个领域。

自动化测试和验证阶段是我正在研究的另一个领域。 我如何创建一个自动化程序，在交付之前执行手动审核过程，以检查可访问性、移动设备上的外观或是否存在任何回归等内容？ 这样我的 QA 阶段就会继续缩短。

如何开始

如果您愿意，我正在开源我的循环设置供您尝试。 每个人的过程都不同，所以您甚至可能想从头开始。

作为第一步，我建议在写任何其他内容之前写下“完成”的样子。 我的协议中的每一个好的决定都来自于被迫精确定义一个状态：任务已完成、绿色 CI 和经过批准的 AI 代码审查。 从那里你可以从“完成”开始慢慢锻炼。 在前端，您如何从任务或问题到完成的 PR，以及在后端如何确保一切都准备好供您审核。

如果您尝试一下，我很想看看它对您有何作用！ 请联系我并告诉我。
